sections.html:
Horry County takes in the Grand Strand, the Atlantic coastline around Myrtle Beach, and also reaches inland to places like Conway, Loris and Aynor. Population has climbed from 269,291 in 2010 to 351,029 in 2020, with 427,551 estimated for 2025. Retirees and second-home buyers drive much of that growth.

A large share of the housing is condos, rentals and vacation property. Owners who live out of state, or who inherited a beach-area unit, often find that managing it from a distance is the hardest part, and that is when a quick sale starts to make sense.

Each October 1 the county mails real property notices to the January 1 owner of record. The whole amount must be paid by the next January 15. If you mail a check, the postmark on the envelope is what counts, and a bill that went astray will not save you from a penalty.

Late charges land on January 16 (3 percent), February 2 (7 percent more) and March 17 (5 percent more), a schedule found in S.C. Code 12-45-180. Your notice lists the dollar figures.

  • Treasurer's line for payments: 843-428-2126.
  • You can pay at the Treasurer's Office, by mail, through a night deposit box, online or by phone. Cards cost an extra convenience fee.

Real property owners can enroll in an installment plan by applying before January 15 of the tax year. Escrowed property and personal vehicles are left out.

PaymentDue dateAmount
Advance payment 1February 1516.67 percent of last year's tax
Advance payment 2April 1516.67 percent of last year's tax

Advance payment 4August 1516.67 percent of last year's tax
Advance payment 5October 1516.67 percent of last year's tax

The remaining balance is billed by November 15, and no installment is taken after October 15. An application can be denied for outstanding taxes, a bank escrow account, or because you do not own the property. If you plan to sell mid-year, ask the Treasurer how the plan fits with your closing.

sections.h2: Reassessment and the legal residence rate
sections.html:
Horry County reappraises on a multi-year cycle, working for four years and implementing in the fifth. Ask the Assessor which year comes next. Increases from a countywide reappraisal are capped at 15 percent over five years, but the cap does not protect the year an assessable transfer first becomes taxable, and a sale is the usual trigger.

  • Legal residence status, the 4 percent assessment, must be applied for between January 1 and January 15.
  • A change in use has to be reported to the Assessor within six months.
  • The $50,000 homestead deduction covers owners 65 or older, the blind, the disabled and surviving spouses. First-time applicants file in person at the Auditor's Office, 843-915-5051.

Ask for a conference in writing within 90 days of the assessment notice. In a year with no notice, you can appeal whenever you like, and an appeal filed before the first penalty date counts for that tax year.

The letter should give your name, the Map-Block-Parcel number, the value you think is correct and why. The legal basis is S.C. Code 12-60-2510. When agricultural land changes use, roll-back taxes apply for the year of change and the four years before.

sections.h2: Delinquent taxes and the tax sale
sections.html:
On March 17 real property taxes become delinquent. Notices follow around April 1, certified notices come roughly 30 days after that, and levy notices are posted at delinquent properties, usually sometime from May through October.

Three Thursdays in a row carry the sale advertisement. After the sale, you have 12 months to redeem. The Delinquent Tax Office, 1301 Second Avenue in Conway, takes calls at (843) 915-5472 and keeps weekday hours of 8 am to 5 pm. Look for the sale date and location in a November newspaper ad.

When the property changes hands, state and county recording tax on the deed is $1.85 per $500 of value, set by Title 12, Chapter 24.

Water covers about 9 percent of the county, and the Waccamaw and Pee Dee rivers and the Intracoastal Waterway all run through it. The county's flood plan says Hurricane Florence damaged more than 2,000 buildings and closed more than 460 roads. Bucksport, Longs, Red Bluff and Socastee are named as target communities.

Flood maps matter at sale time. In Socastee, fewer than 20 percent of damaged buildings (96 of 565) sat inside the Special Flood Hazard Area on the maps in effect. Check the flood zone and the insurance claim history for your house before you list it. If the house is damaged or flood-prone, a buyer who pays cash and takes it as-is can purchase it without asking you to rebuild.

sections.h2: Selling when you live elsewhere or owe tax
sections.html:
Living out of state need not slow you down, because nearly every step works over the phone. The Treasurer, 843-428-2126, quotes a payoff that rises at each penalty date. The Auditor, 843-915-5051, can say whether a homestead deduction sits on the account, and the Assessor can explain your legal residence rate.

Then read the recorded deed and confirm it carries the seller's name. A unit passed down in the family generally needs the estate settled first. The county is paid from your proceeds by the title company at the closing table.

A cash buyer who takes the property as it stands removes repairs, showings and loan delays. Two questions are worth raising early with the Assessor: whether roll-back taxes apply to farmland, and whether a change of use has been reported.

Keep the Treasurer's receipt, your closing statement and the deed copy together. The following year's bill will go to the new owner of record, so the Assessor needs your forwarding address if you are still receiving mail for the old one.

sections.h2: Before you list: a short checklist
sections.html:
1. Look up your account with the Treasurer and note the balance and the date it was quoted.
  2. Confirm the legal residence rate and any homestead deduction are on file. If they are not, ask the Assessor and the Auditor how a sale affects them.
  3. Pull the recorded deed and compare names, the tax map number and the Map-Block-Parcel number.
  4. Check flood zone status and past insurance claims, especially near Socastee or Bucksport.
  5. Ask whether any use changes were reported to the Assessor in the last six months.

A sale is usually the event that triggers a fresh valuation and lifts the 15 percent cap, so the next owner's bill may look quite different from yours. Telling your buyer about that early prevents an unpleasant surprise after closing.

faqs.q: What is the payment deadline for real property in Horry County?
faqs.a: January 15, with notices mailed on October 1. Penalties kick in on January 16, February 2 and March 17.

faqs.q: Is there an installment option in Horry County?
faqs.a: Yes, for real property when your application arrives before January 15. Five payments of 16.67 percent of last year's tax run from February through October, and the rest is billed by November 15.

faqs.q: When can I apply for the 4 percent rate in Horry County?
faqs.a: File in that window, January 1 to January 15. The home must be yours, and your primary residence, on January 1.

faqs.q: What is the redemption period after an Horry County tax sale?
faqs.a: One year, counted from the day of the sale. Whoever owned the house, a lender or a grantee can recover it by paying the taxes and costs of the sale.

faqs.q: Do Horry County homes face flood risk?
faqs.a: Some do. The county's plan singles out Bucksport, Longs, Red Bluff and Socastee, so look up the flood zone and insurance history before listing.
